question_text:
A 58-year-old woman attends a Melbourne general practice for a repeat prescription of transdermal oestradiol. She has no breast symptoms. Her mother is alive at 84, and an aunt developed breast cancer at 71. Her last BreastScreen mammogram, 26 months ago, was normal but reported heterogeneously dense breast tissue. She asks whether she should have MRI or ultrasound instead of another mammogram. Examination is normal.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Arrange her next BreastScreen mammogram now.
Replace mammography with annual screening MRI.
Replace mammography with screening ultrasound because of breast density.
Wait until age 65 before further screening.
Order CA 15-3 and image only if it is elevated.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
A. Arrange her next BreastScreen mammogram now.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
BreastScreen Australia offers biennial mammography to women aged 50–74, with access also available to eligible women aged 40–49 and those over 74. At 58, she is overdue for routine screening. Breast density can reduce mammographic sensitivity, but density alone does not make MRI or ultrasound the routine population screening replacement.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Correct. Her two-year screening interval has elapsed.
B. MRI is not the routine population screening test for an average-risk woman with this history.
C. Ultrasound is not a routine substitute for mammography based on density alone.
D. There is no reason to defer screening until 65.
E. CA 15-3 is not a population screening test for breast cancer.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Apply Australian breast screening eligibility and distinguish breast density from a high-risk surveillance indication.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Apply Australian breast screening eligibility and distinguish breast density from a high-risk surveillance indication.

EVIDENCE
BreastScreen Australia: https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/breastscreen-australia

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: MRI is not the routine population screening test for an average-risk woman with this history.

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: There is no reason to defer screening until 65.

question_text:
A 46-year-old woman in Adelaide asks her GP for a BreastScreen referral after a friend says free mammograms are only available from age 50. She has no breast symptoms. Her sister had a fibroadenoma removed at 29, with no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Examination is normal.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: She must wait until age 50 before she can access BreastScreen.
She can access BreastScreen now, although routine invitations generally begin at 50.
She requires annual mammography because she requested screening before 50.
She should have annual screening ultrasound instead.
A normal examination means no imaging is needed until 50.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
B. She can access BreastScreen now, although routine invitations generally begin at 50.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
Women aged 40–49 can access BreastScreen Australia, although the program routinely invites women aged 50–74. A fibroadenoma in a relative is not equivalent to a family history of breast cancer.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Incorrect. Access is not restricted to women aged 50 or older.
B. Correct. She can discuss and arrange screening now.
C. Requesting screening early does not automatically establish a need for annual imaging.
D. Ultrasound is not the standard population screening alternative.
E. Clinical examination cannot replace appropriate screening mammography.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Explain the difference between routine invitation age and program access.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Explain the difference between routine invitation age and program access.

EVIDENCE
BreastScreen Australia: https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/breastscreen-australia

question_text:
A 44-year-old woman in Brisbane reports a firm lump in her left breast that has persisted for three weeks. She planned to wait until she reached screening age. Examination confirms a 2 cm firm, mobile mass without palpable axillary nodes. A BreastScreen appointment is available in 10 days, and the nurse suggests using it to avoid delay.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Use the screening appointment and act only if the report is abnormal.
Reassure her that a mobile lump can be reviewed in six months.
Arrange prompt diagnostic assessment of the breast lump.
Start tamoxifen and repeat examination in three months.
Order CA 15-3 and a chest X-ray before deciding about imaging.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
C. Arrange prompt diagnostic assessment of the breast lump.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
A palpable breast mass requires diagnostic assessment, commonly involving clinical examination, age-appropriate diagnostic imaging and tissue sampling when indicated. A population screening appointment is not a substitute for investigating a symptom.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Screening pathways are designed for asymptomatic people and may not provide the necessary diagnostic work-up.
B. Mobility does not reliably exclude malignancy; delay is inappropriate.
C. Correct. Arrange prompt diagnostic assessment.
D. Tamoxifen should not be started empirically for an undiagnosed breast mass.
E. Tumour markers and chest X-ray are not the initial diagnostic pathway for an isolated breast lump.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Recognise when symptoms override routine screening eligibility.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Recognise when symptoms override routine screening eligibility.

EVIDENCE
Cancer Australia: https://www.canceraustralia.gov.au/

question_text:
A 76-year-old woman in Perth remains independent, drives and has well-controlled hypertension and osteoarthritis. She has attended BreastScreen every two years since age 52. Her last mammogram was normal 18 months ago. A friend tells her that breast screening is prohibited after age 74. She has no symptoms.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Arrange annual MRI because routine invitations have stopped.
Continue mandatory annual mammography until age 80.
Replace mammography with annual clinical examination.
Explain that routine invitations stop after 74, but she may discuss and choose further screening.
Explain that mammography is contraindicated after age 74.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
D. Explain that routine invitations stop after 74, but she may discuss and choose further screening.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
Routine BreastScreen invitations target women aged 50–74. Women older than 74 may still access screening, but the potential benefits, harms, life expectancy, health status and preferences should inform the decision.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. MRI is not the automatic replacement for routine mammography.
B. Annual mammography is not mandatory.
C. Clinical examination alone is not an equivalent screening substitute.
D. Correct. Use shared decision-making about further screening.
E. Screening is not categorically contraindicated solely because of age.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Apply individualised decision-making when a patient is outside the routine screening invitation age.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Apply individualised decision-making when a patient is outside the routine screening invitation age.

EVIDENCE
BreastScreen Australia: https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/breastscreen-australia

question_text:
A 36-year-old woman in Sydney is eight weeks pregnant. Genetic testing has identified a pathogenic BRCA1 variant, and her mother developed breast cancer at 38. She has no breast symptoms. A midwife tells her that breast screening is unnecessary until population screening age and can be reconsidered after childbearing.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Wait until age 50 for routine BreastScreen invitations.
Use annual ultrasound as the sole long-term surveillance plan.
Arrange prophylactic bilateral mastectomy immediately, without further assessment.
Defer all risk management until she has completed childbearing.
Refer for specialist familial cancer and high-risk breast surveillance advice, taking pregnancy into account.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
E. Refer for specialist familial cancer and high-risk breast surveillance advice, taking pregnancy into account.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
A pathogenic BRCA1 variant and a strong early-onset family history warrant specialist risk management. The surveillance plan must be individualised and account for pregnancy, imaging choices, risk-reducing options and reproductive preferences.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Average-risk screening ages are not sufficient for this high-risk patient.
B. Ultrasound alone is not automatically an adequate lifelong surveillance plan.
C. Risk-reducing surgery requires specialist counselling and shared decision-making; it is not an automatic immediate intervention.
D. Risk assessment should not be postponed until childbearing is complete.
E. Correct. Refer to an appropriate familial cancer/high-risk service.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Distinguish population screening from surveillance for inherited cancer susceptibility.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Distinguish population screening from surveillance for inherited cancer susceptibility.

EVIDENCE
Cancer Australia: https://www.canceraustralia.gov.au/

question_text:
A 62-year-old asymptomatic man in Hobart asks to join the same BreastScreen program as his wife. He has no breast symptoms or family history and is willing to pay privately if necessary. Examination is normal.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Routine population breast screening is not offered to asymptomatic men; assess any future symptoms promptly.
Enrol him in biennial mammography because he is older than 50.
Arrange annual breast ultrasound as the male equivalent of BreastScreen.
Measure CA 15-3 every two years.
Prescribe tamoxifen as a standard male breast cancer prevention program.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
A. Routine population breast screening is not offered to asymptomatic men; assess any future symptoms promptly.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
BreastScreen Australia is a population screening program for women. An asymptomatic man without a specific high-risk indication is not enrolled in an equivalent routine population program.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Correct. Explain the program scope and safety-net new symptoms.
B. Male sex and age alone do not create eligibility for routine BreastScreen.
C. Ultrasound is not a standard population screening substitute.
D. CA 15-3 is not a screening test.

question_text:
A 47-year-old man in Canberra has no bowel symptoms and no relevant family history. His wife, aged 52, has received a National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kit. He has never screened and asks whether he is too young because he remembers the program starting at 50.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: He must wait until age 50 before any program screening is possible.
He can request a free bowel screening kit now; routine automatic mail-outs begin at age 50.
He should undergo colonoscopy because his wife received a kit.
He should request a kit only if he develops rectal bleeding.
He should have annual CEA testing until age 50.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
B. He can request a free bowel screening kit now; routine automatic mail-outs begin at age 50.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
Eligible Australians aged 45–49 can request their first free kit. People aged 50–74 are routinely mailed a kit every two years. Screening is intended for people without symptoms.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Incorrect. Eligibility begins at 45.
B. Correct. He can request his first kit.
C. His wife's invitation does not indicate that he needs colonoscopy.
D. Screening should occur before symptoms arise; symptoms require diagnostic assessment instead.
E. CEA is not a population screening test.

question_text:
A 63-year-old woman in Darwin receives a bowel screening kit. She had haemorrhoids banded six years ago and has had no bleeding since. She has no weight loss, change in bowel habit or known anaemia. She asks whether she should discard the kit and arrange colonoscopy because a friend of similar age had one.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Arrange colonoscopy because everyone over 60 requires it instead of a kit.
Keep the kit until she notices bleeding.
Complete and return the kit if she remains asymptomatic and otherwise eligible.
Request CEA before deciding whether to screen.
Use the kit only if a blood test demonstrates anaemia.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
C. Complete and return the kit if she remains asymptomatic and otherwise eligible.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
An eligible, asymptomatic person aged 45–74 should participate in biennial screening. Remote, successfully treated haemorrhoids do not by themselves require colonoscopy instead of screening. New symptoms or a relevant personal or family history would warrant individual assessment.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Colonoscopy is not automatically required solely because of age.
B. Screening is intended before symptoms develop.
C. Correct. Complete the kit if no exclusion or alternative pathway applies.
D. CEA is not a screening test.
E. Screening does not require anaemia.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Distinguish routine screening from investigation prompted by symptoms or increased risk.

KEY TAKEAWAY

question_text:
A 55-year-old man in Newcastle has a positive faecal immunochemical screening test. He feels well, has no rectal bleeding and has a haemoglobin concentration of 148 g/L. He ate rare steak before collecting the sample and wants to repeat the test after dietary restriction, as he remembers being advised with an older stool test.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the kit after six weeks of dietary restriction.
Wait until the next routine two-year screening invitation.
Order CEA and investigate only if it is elevated.
Arrange appropriate diagnostic follow-up, usually colonoscopy.
Start oral iron and repeat the kit if haemoglobin falls.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
D. Arrange appropriate diagnostic follow-up, usually colonoscopy.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
A positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test requires follow-up to investigate the source of blood. A normal haemoglobin concentration and absence of symptoms do not exclude colorectal neoplasia. Dietary restrictions associated with older guaiac-based tests do not justify repeating a positive FIT instead of investigating it.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Repeating the test can delay definitive investigation.
B. A positive result requires follow-up now, not at the next routine interval.
C. CEA cannot exclude colorectal cancer or replace colonoscopy.
D. Correct. Arrange diagnostic follow-up and assess the patient clinically.
E. Iron is not indicated solely to manage a positive screening test.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Manage a positive bowel screening result without using repeat screening to avoid diagnostic investigation.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Manage a positive bowel screening result without using repeat screening to avoid diagnostic investigation.

EVIDENCE

question_text:
A 60-year-old man in Geelong reports bright-red rectal bleeding on most days for three weeks. His haemoglobin is 132 g/L. Rectal examination shows no fissure or prolapsed haemorrhoid. He has a bowel screening kit due this month and asks to complete it before deciding whether to seek further care.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give him the kit and discharge him if the result is negative.
Repeat the kit after the bleeding has stopped for six weeks.
Order CEA and arrange colonoscopy only if it is elevated.
Reassure him that bright-red bleeding is usually haemorrhoidal.
Arrange prompt diagnostic assessment for the rectal bleeding rather than relying on screening.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
E. Arrange prompt diagnostic assessment for the rectal bleeding rather than relying on screening.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
Rectal bleeding is a symptom requiring clinical assessment. The clinician should determine the urgency and appropriate investigation based on age, persistence, examination, blood results and other risk factors. A screening kit is not an adequate substitute.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. A negative screening test does not exclude significant disease in a symptomatic patient.
B. Waiting for symptoms to resolve may delay diagnosis.
C. CEA is not a diagnostic gatekeeper for colonoscopy.
D. Bright-red blood does not establish a benign cause.
E. Correct. Investigate the symptom through the appropriate diagnostic pathway.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Recognise that symptomatic patients should not be managed solely through population screening.

KEY TAKEAWAY

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman in Wollongong had a complete colonoscopy 14 months ago, during which a 6 mm tubular adenoma was removed. Her specialist documented a five-year surveillance interval. She has no bowel symptoms. A program screening kit arrives, and she asks whether she should complete it as well.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Do not complete the program kit now; follow the individualised colonoscopy surveillance plan.
Complete the kit because a government invitation overrides the specialist plan.
Replace the planned surveillance colonoscopy with biennial kits.
Order CEA and cancel all further bowel surveillance if it is normal.
Start annual kits because an adenoma was previously found.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
A. Do not complete the program kit now; follow the individualised colonoscopy surveillance plan.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
A recent colonoscopy and personal history of adenoma may make routine population screening inappropriate at that time. The patient should follow the documented surveillance plan and clarify any uncertainty with the treating clinician.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Correct. A recent colonoscopy and planned surveillance take precedence over automatically repeating population screening.
B. Invitations do not override individual clinical circumstances.
C. A screening kit does not replace indicated colonoscopic surveillance.
D. A normal CEA cannot exclude colorectal cancer.
E. A previous adenoma does not automatically mandate annual FIT.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Reconcile population screening invitations with an existing individual surveillance plan.

KEY TAKEAWAY

question_text:
A 78-year-old man in Launceston is independent and has no bowel symptoms. His younger brother has just completed a mailed screening kit. His son reads that the national program covers people up to age 80 and asks the GP to order another kit for his father.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Request an automatic program kit because he is fit and well.
Explain that he is outside the program's routine age range; discuss individual options if appropriate.
Arrange urgent colonoscopy because no kit has arrived.
Tell him that no bowel investigation is appropriate after age 74, even if symptoms arise.
Order annual CEA instead of a screening kit.

CORRECT ANSWER
B. Explain that he is outside the program's routine age range; discuss individual options if appropriate.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program covers eligible people aged 45–74. Above 74, there is no routine program invitation; any further screening decision should consider benefits, harms, health status and preferences. New symptoms still require assessment.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Fitness alone does not extend routine program eligibility.
B. Correct. Discuss individual options rather than assuming automatic eligibility.
C. Absence of a kit is not itself an indication for colonoscopy.
D. Age does not remove the need to investigate future symptoms.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman in Melbourne attends with her mother, who began Pap smears at age 18. The daughter has never had sexual contact, has no vaginal bleeding or pelvic symptoms, and received HPV vaccination at school. Her mother requests a Cervical Screening Test.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Begin two-yearly Pap smears because that was the previous recommendation.
Arrange colposcopy before she becomes sexually active.
Explain that routine cervical screening is not due at age 22.
Take a self-collected HPV sample and repeat it in 12 months.
Explain that HPV vaccination means she will never need screening.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
C. Explain that routine cervical screening is not due at age 22.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
Australia's National Cervical Screening Program routinely invites eligible people with a cervix aged 25–74 who have ever been sexually active. A 22-year-old without symptoms is not due for routine screening. Vaccination does not eliminate the need for screening once eligible.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. The program no longer uses routine two-yearly Pap smears.
B. Colposcopy is not indicated in an asymptomatic, unscreened person solely because of age.
C. Correct. Explain the current starting age and provide future recall advice.
D. Self-collection is not a reason to screen below the routine age in this asymptomatic scenario.
E. HPV vaccination reduces risk but does not replace screening.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Apply the current cervical screening starting age and distinguish vaccination from screening.

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman in Brisbane completed HPV vaccination at school. She has had sexual contact, has no symptoms and has never had a Cervical Screening Test. A pharmacy clinic tells her that vaccination protects her for life and she can ignore screening invitations.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Arrange annual Pap smears because vaccination changes the interval.
Defer screening until age 30 because she was vaccinated.
Arrange colposcopy as the first screening test.
She should have a Cervical Screening Test now.
Cancel all future screening because vaccination is sufficient.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
D. She should have a Cervical Screening Test now.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
An eligible 28-year-old who has ever been sexually active should participate in the National Cervical Screening Program. HPV vaccination reduces the risk of infection from covered types but does not eliminate all oncogenic HPV risk.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Annual Pap smears are not the routine current pathway.
B. There is no need to delay until age 30.

question_text:
A 49-year-old woman in Mildura has no bowel symptoms and no known family history of colorectal cancer. She has never participated in screening. Her 51-year-old neighbour received a National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kit automatically last month. She asks whether she should wait for her own kit to arrive.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Explain that automatic invitations begin at 45 and she should wait for the mail-out.
Explain that she cannot participate until age 50.
Explain that she can request her first free kit now; automatic mail-outs generally begin at age 50.
Arrange colonoscopy as the first test for every person aged 49.
Advise her to wait until symptoms develop before screening.
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER
C. Explain that she can request her first free kit now; automatic mail-outs generally begin at age 50.

CLINICAL EXPLANATION
Eligible Australians aged 45–49 can request their first free bowel screening kit. Automatic mail-outs are generally provided every two years to eligible people aged 50–74. A 49-year-old does not need to wait until age 50 to begin participating.

OPTION-BY-OPTION ANALYSIS
A. Automatic mail-outs do not routinely start at 45.
B. Eligibility begins at 45, not 50.
C. Correct. Explain how she can request her first kit.
D. Colonoscopy is not the default first test for every asymptomatic 49-year-old.
E. Screening is intended to detect disease before symptoms develop.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Apply the current age-based access and invitation rules of the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Apply the current age-based access and invitation rules of the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program.

EVIDENCE
